title: Judging without deciding
primary_topics: Foundational DAP-mootness 'moot and academic' doctrinal column February 9, 2014

SolGen Francis Jardeleza arguments (Harvard-educated bar-topnotcher counsel of Republic): (1) President 'authorized the disbursements under the DAP' (2) 'disbursements [had] an appropriation cover' (3) 'government [had] sufficient savings to support these disbursements' → 'there were actual savings... ergo, DAP is constitutional'

Jardeleza 'functus officio' mooting argument: 'circumstances that justified creation of DAP no longer obtain... DAP... lapsed into complete disuse in 2013 and became functus officio... DAP... no longer exists, thereby mooting the present cases'
Should Court adjudicate by dismissing without deciding because moot-and-academic? Key procedural-constitutional question

General rule: Philippine and US courts decide 'on their merit' only with 'actual case or controversy' involving 'conflict of legal rights... susceptible of judicial resolution... not mooted by supervening events'; unlike European judiciaries, our judges not authorized to render 'advisory opinions... do not adjudicate academic or hypothetical or anticipatory questions, no matter how intellectually challenging'

Lis-mota doctrine: 'courts will not pass upon a constitutional question unless it is the lis mota of the case, or if the case can be disposed of on some other grounds,' like its having become moot and academic
'Capable of repetition' exception: jurisprudence has carved clear exceptions, the most cited being 'when the case is capable of repetition yet evading review'

David v. Arroyo (May 3, 2006, Justice Angelina Sandoval Gutierrez): PP 1017 'state of national emergency' Feb 24 2006 → warrantless arrests (Randy David, Akbayan Roland Llamas, Tribune/Malaya pillage) → lifted March 3 2006 → Court 11-3 voted 'capable of repetition while evading judicial review by expediency of its lifting'; Gutierrez ponencia 'rhapsodized': 'Court has duty to formulate guiding and controlling constitutional precepts, doctrines and rules... symbolic function of educating bench, bar, military and police'

Lacson v. Perez (May 10, 2001, Justice Jose A. R. Melo): Arroyo Edsa-3 'state of rebellion' Proclamation 38 → lifted May 6, 2001 → Court 7-4 threw out petitions because lifting mooted them (petitioners not arrested without warrant, suffered no damage; nature changed to declaratory relief over which SC had no original jurisdiction); nevertheless 'enjoined [government] from arresting petitioners... without required judicial warrants...'

Sanlakas v. Exec. Sec. (Feb 4, 2004, Justice Dante O. Tinga): Arroyo Proclamation 427 July 27 2003 'state of rebellion' after 300 military personnel Oakwood Premier 'demanded resignation of President'; lifted Aug 1 2003 → Tinga ponencia tackled constitutional issues head-on, held that while Constitution does not expressly grant President power to declare state of rebellion, such 'springs in the main from her powers as chief executive and... draws strength from her Commander-in-Chief powers'; vote-breakdown 3 unconditional + 1 conditional separate opinion + 3 'in the result' + 3 dismiss-on-mootness + 2 dissent-as-void + 1 on leave + 1 vacant seat; 'Readers may draw their own conclusions' + 'As retired jurist would not venture opinion till after DAP cases are heard in full' + Feb 18 oral argument continuation + 'Abangan!' close
sub_topics: Solicitor General Francis Jardeleza, Harvard-educated and bar-topnotcher counsel of Republic
Argued in Supreme Court that (1) President 'authorized the disbursements under the DAP'
(2) 'disbursements [had] an appropriation cover'
(3) 'government [had] sufficient savings to support these disbursements'
In short, he concluded, 'there were actual savings which the President himself authorized to augment existing items in the GAA'
Ergo, DAP is constitutional
Nonetheless, he added, 'circumstances that justified creation of DAP no longer obtain'
'DAP... lapsed into complete disuse in 2013 and became functus officio'
'DAP... no longer exists, thereby mooting the present cases'
Should Court adjudicate cases by dismissing them without deciding constitutional issues, because they have become moot and academic?
As rule, Philippine (and US) courts decide issues 'on their merit' only when they present 'actual case or controversy'
That involves 'conflict of legal rights... susceptible of judicial resolution... not mooted by supervening events'
Unlike judiciaries in Europe, our judges are not authorized to render 'advisory opinions'
'They do not adjudicate academic or hypothetical or anticipatory questions, no matter how intellectually challenging'
Moreover, 'courts will not pass upon a constitutional question unless it is the lis mota of the case'
Or if case can be disposed of on some other grounds, like its having become moot and academic
Jurisprudence, however, has carved clear exceptions to this general rule
Most cited being 'when the case is capable of repetition yet evading review'
Good example is David v. Arroyo (May 3, 2006, per Justice Angelina Sandoval Gutierrez)
On Feb 24, 2006, then President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo issued Presidential Proclamation 1017 declaring 'state of national emergency'
That resulted in, among others, warrantless arrest of many, including columnist Randy David and Akbayan president Roland Llamas
As well as in pillage of Tribune and Malaya
Week later, on March 3, 2006, President Arroyo lifted PP 1017
Thus, government asked Court to dismiss petitions assailing constitutionality of PP 1017 on ground that lifting had mooted constitutional issues
Court, voting 11-3 (with one on leave), refused
Reasoning that while lifting rendered issues moot and academic, President's act is capable of repetition while evading judicial review by expediency of its lifting
Constitutional rights have been violated and private parties suffered as result
Gutierrez ponencia rhapsodized: 'Court has duty to formulate guiding and controlling constitutional precepts, doctrines and rules'
'It has symbolic function of educating bench and bar, and in present petitions, military and police on extent of protection given by constitutional guarantees'
At other times, Court followed general rule
In Lacson v. Perez (May 10, 2001, per Justice Jose A. R. Melo)
President Arroyo, 'faced by angry and violent mob... assaulting and attempting to break into Malacañang' (in what some call 'Edsa 3')
Issued Proclamation 38 declaring 'state of rebellion...'
On May 6, 2001, she lifted proclamation
Thus, government asked Court to dismiss all petitions brought by Panfilo Lacson et al.
Challenging constitutionality of presidential order
Voting 7-4 (with four on leave), Court threw out petitions because lifting rendered them moot and academic
Saying petitioners, not having been arrested without warrant as they had feared, suffered no damage
Further, mooting changed their nature to one for declaratory relief over which Supreme Court had no original jurisdiction
Nevertheless, it 'enjoined [government] from arresting petitioners... without required judicial warrants...'
Later on, in Sanlakas v. Executive Secretary (Feb 4, 2004, per Justice Dante O. Tinga)
President Arroyo issued Proclamation 427 on July 27, 2003
Declaring (again) 'state of rebellion'
After some 300 military personnel 'stormed into Oakwood Premier apartments in Makati City... bewailing corruption...'
And 'demanded, among other things, resignation of President...'
Though proclamation was lifted on Aug 1, 2003, thereby mooting petitions
Tinga ponencia tackled constitutional issues head-on
Held that while Constitution does not expressly grant President power to declare state of rebellion
Such prerogative 'springs in the main from her powers as chief executive and... draws strength from her Commander-in-Chief powers'
Three justices joined ponencia unconditionally; one conditionally via separate opinion; three others only 'in the result'
Three voted to dismiss petitions on sole ground of mootness while two dissented, saying proclamation was void
One was on leave. One seat was vacant
Foregoing shows Court tackled 'moot and academic' defense in varying ways depending on peculiarities of each case
Readers may draw their own conclusions
As retired jurist, CJP would not venture opinion till after DAP cases are heard in full
Note that oral argument will continue on Feb 18
Abangan!

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the foundational explainer of the moot-and-academic doctrine + capable-of-repetition-yet-evading-review exception, set up to anchor his forthcoming DAP-arc commentary. SolGen Francis Jardeleza, the Harvard-educated and bar-topnotcher counsel of the Republic, argued in the SC that (1) the President 'authorized the disbursements under the DAP,' (2) the 'disbursements [had] an appropriation cover,' and (3) 'the government [had] sufficient savings to support these disbursements.' Moot and academic: in short, he concluded, 'there were actual savings which the President himself authorized to augment existing items in the GAA' -- ergo, the DAP is constitutional. Nonetheless, he added, 'the circumstances that justified the creation of DAP no longer obtain... DAP... lapsed into complete disuse in 2013 and became functus officio... DAP... no longer exists, thereby mooting the present cases.' Should the Court adjudicate the cases by dismissing them without deciding the constitutional issues, because they have become moot and academic? As a rule, Philippine (and US) courts decide issues 'on their merit' only when they present an 'actual case or controversy' that involves a 'conflict of legal rights... susceptible of judicial resolution... not mooted by supervening events.' Unlike judiciaries in Europe, our judges are not authorized to render 'advisory opinions... They do not adjudicate academic or hypothetical or anticipatory questions, no matter how intellectually challenging.' Moreover, 'courts will not pass upon a constitutional question unless it is the lis mota of the case, or if the case can be disposed of on some other grounds,' like its having become moot and academic. Capable of repetition: jurisprudence, however, has carved clear exceptions to this general rule, the most cited being 'when the case is capable of repetition yet evading review.' A good example is David v. Arroyo (May 3, 2006, per Justice Angelina Sandoval Gutierrez): on Feb 24, 2006, then President GMA issued PP 1017 declaring a 'state of national emergency' that resulted in, among others, the warrantless arrest of many, including columnist Randy David and Akbayan president Roland Llamas, as well as in the pillage of the Tribune and the Malaya. A week later, on March 3, 2006, GMA lifted PP 1017; thus, the government asked the Court to dismiss the petitions assailing the constitutionality of PP 1017 on the ground that the lifting had mooted the constitutional issues. The Court, voting 11-3 (with one on leave), refused, reasoning that while the lifting rendered the issues moot and academic, the President's act is capable of repetition while evading judicial review by the expediency of its lifting -- constitutional rights have been violated and private parties suffered as a result. The Gutierrez ponencia rhapsodized: 'The Court has the duty to formulate guiding and controlling constitutional precepts, doctrines and rules; it has the symbolic function of educating the bench and the bar, and in the present petitions, the military and the police on the extent of the protection given by constitutional guarantees.' At other times, the Court followed the general rule. In Lacson v. Perez (May 10, 2001, per Justice Jose A. R. Melo), GMA, 'faced by an angry and violent mob... assaulting and attempting to break into Malacañang' (in what some call 'Edsa 3'), issued Proclamation 38 declaring a 'state of rebellion.' On May 6, 2001, she lifted the proclamation, thus the government asked the Court to dismiss all petitions brought by Panfilo Lacson et al. challenging the constitutionality of the presidential order. Voting 7-4 (with four on leave), the Court threw out the petitions because the lifting rendered them moot and academic, saying that the petitioners, not having been arrested without warrant as they had feared, suffered no damage; further, the mooting changed their nature to one for declaratory relief over which the SC had no original jurisdiction; nevertheless, it 'enjoined [the government] from arresting petitioners... without the required judicial warrants...' Later on, in Sanlakas v. Executive Secretary (Feb 4, 2004, per Justice Dante O. Tinga), President Arroyo issued Proclamation 427 on July 27, 2003, declaring (again) a 'state of rebellion' after some 300 military personnel 'stormed into the Oakwood Premier apartments in Makati City... bewailing corruption...' and 'demanded, among other things, the resignation of the President.' Though the proclamation was lifted on Aug 1, 2003, thereby mooting the petitions, the Tinga ponencia tackled the constitutional issues head-on -- it held that while the Constitution does not expressly grant the President the power to declare a state of rebellion, such prerogative 'springs in the main from her powers as chief executive and... draws strength from her Commander-in-Chief powers.' Three justices joined the ponencia unconditionally; one conditionally via a separate opinion; and three others only 'in the result'; three voted to dismiss the petitions on the sole ground of mootness while two dissented, saying the proclamation was void; one was on leave; one seat was vacant. The foregoing shows that the Court tackled the 'moot and academic' defense in varying ways depending on the peculiarities of each case -- readers may draw their own conclusions; as a retired jurist, CJ would not venture an opinion till after the DAP cases are heard in full; note that the oral argument will continue on Feb 18; Abangan!
